newsitem.title: CHINA: Aid agency sees malnutrition, deaths in N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Aid agency sees malnutrition, deaths in N.Korea.

text.p: North Korea is sliding into famine with reports of deaths of children from malnutrition and farmers eating powdered wood to fill out their diet, an official of the international aid agency Caritas said on Tuesday.

"The overall situation is just going down," Kathi Zellweger, director of international cooperation for the Hong Kong branch of Caritas said in an interview after visiting the reclusive Stalinist state.
"It's like a ladder I'm climbing down and I don't where the bottom rung is," she said referring to visits in recent years.

A day earlier the United Nations' food aid agency called for large-scale emergency aid to North Korea to avert a famine that could turn into "one of the biggest humanitarian disasters of our lifetime".

On a visit to areas devastated by unprecedented floods in 1995 and again in 1996 when entire crops were destroyed, Zellweger said she saw fewer children in schools, listless infants and heard of deaths from malnutrition.

The headmistress of a school in one county described the situation as the worst since the Japanese occupation of World War Two, an invasion regarded by Koreans as one of the darkest points in their history, she said.
"She said she had never before experienced children dying of malnutrition, but said she knew of five cases," Zellweger said.

Fewer children were able to attend kindergartens and nurseries because these could no longer provide lunch, and hospitals too were virtually empty because of shortages of medicine and a lack of food, she said.
"I feel it's a famine in slow motion," she said.
"If no major food aid is going in fairly soon it will just go further down and could deteriorate very, very rapidly," she said. "We can only hope for the best, we have to prepare for the worst."

The U.N. World Food Programme launched a $95.5 million appeal this month for 203,000 tonnes of emergency food for North Korea. The agency said on Monday it had received just one-third of the money and estimated North Korea needed 1.3 million tonnes of additional food to meet its basic needs in 1997.

Kellweger said local officials told her they distributed 100-350 grams (3.5-12 ounces) of rice per adult per day, although some areas said they had been unable to distribute since mid-March. That compared with the minimum recommended by Caritas of 450 grams (1.0 lb) per person per day.
"Officials say they will run out of food fairly soon... They asked me several times to look at quantity and not at quality of the food aid we bring in," she sid.
To make up for the shortages in the diet, people were eating anything they could find, she said.
Women and children collected edible plants and she said she saw one mill grinding an oak tree into powder to supplement an inadequate supply of rice and maize.
"I thought at first they were processing firewood, but they said they were making powder out of the wood," she said. "They said it fills you up and gives you a feeling of having eaten."
In one village she entered family homes at lunchtime and saw not a single bowl of rice on dinner tables, only soup.
"I asked one farmer when he ate meat the last time and he said he couldn't remember," she said.

North Korea has said food supplies will run out at the end of April. The WFP estimated there was only enough food to feed the country until June and then its 24 million people would have to wait for the next harvest in October and November.
